To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) GABA receptors are composed of a family of proteins that include a receptor protein (GABAa) which binds GABA with high affinity, a protein that binds benzodiazepines (BZ) with low affinity and which may be a subunit of the receptor (BZ) and an associated protein which binds GABA and which may be the GABA receptor protein (GABAc).

GABA and glycine receptors are pentapeptides, that GABA receptors are composed of two types of subunits, that glutamic acid receptors are composed of four types of subunits and that the glutamic acid receptor is a ligand-gated ion channel.
GABAA receptors have a molecular weight of about 100,000, contain two subunits, and are composed of a protein that binds GABA and a protein that binds a barbiturate.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the biochemical and molecular biological analysis of the mechanisms of action of the major neurotransmitters in the central nervous systems (CNS).
the identification of receptors for amino acid neu­ rotransmitters in the CNS and with the biochemical mechanisms by which they function.
the biochemical characterization of amino acid receptors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have made significant progress toward the understanding of the biochemical mechanisms of action for amino acids as neurotransmitter candidates, but that much remains to be done.
we know a great deal about the receptors for GABA and glycine, but we are just beginning to understand the receptors for glutamic acid.
the receptors for the amino acid transmitters GABA, glycine, and l-glutamic acid have been characterized biochemically.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the receptors for GABA and glycine are similar, but the receptor for glutamic acid is different.
we have made progress in the biochemical identification of receptors for GABA, glycine, and Glu.
we have identified a family of GABA receptors, a glycine receptor, and a glutamate receptor.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can identify and purify receptors for neurotransmitters and that the receptors have properties that are consistent with their function.

the receptor for glycine is an integral membrane protein that has a binding site for glycine, and the receptors for GABA and glutamate are integral membrane proteins that have binding sites for their respective neurotransmitters, and that the receptor for glutamate is a multicomponent complex that includes an integral membrane protein and a separate protein that is not an integral membrane protein.
we are still in the dark ages with respect to the molecular basis of synaptic transmission.
